strengths: The row-update construction is simple and valid: multiplying selected rows by an orthogonal matrix preserves XᵀX and reduces the update to a small optimization problem.
The framework addresses relevant problems involving sparsity and nonnegativity. Including both rotations and reflections covers the full two-dimensional orthogonal group.

The experiments cover four problem classes, ten datasets, and several ranks and regularization settings. They report substantial objective improvements in many settings and include feasibility and smooth stationarity residuals.
weaknesses: The central stationarity claim in Theorem 5.5 is false under the stated assumptions. Appendix B.8 incorrectly infers existence of a common subgradient from existence of a suitable subgradient separately for each block. A counterexample is n=r=3, X=I, A=[[0,1,-1],[-1,0,1],[1,-1,0]], f(X)=-⟨A,X⟩/2, and h(X)=Σ_i|Σ_j X_ij-1|. This h is convex and row-wise separable. Every two-row rotation or reflection is nonimproving, making I an exact block-2 stationary point with H=Q=0 and any positive proximal parameter. However, exp(tA) preserves orthogonality and row sums, and the objective derivative at t=0 is -3. Thus this block-stationary point is not critical, directly contradicting a principal contribution.

The strong-convergence proof has additional substantive errors. Lemma 6.6(b) fails even for h=0, n=3, r=1, k=2, f(x)=x₂, and x=e₁: its left-hand side is 1, while its stated right-hand side is √(2/3). The proof confuses a root mean square with a mean. Appendix B.10 also exchanges Bᵗ and Bᵗ⁺¹ inside an expectation involving Xᵗ⁺¹, although Xᵗ⁺¹ depends on Bᵗ. Consequently, the argument supporting Theorem 6.8 is not valid.

The breakpoint solver is not exact as written. Section 7.1 substitutes t=tan(θ) without covering cos(θ)=0, potentially excluding minimizers. It also discards coordinates with y_i=0, although their ℓ1 contribution λ|x_i|/√(1+t²) depends on t. These errors undermine the exact-subproblem assumption used by OBCD-Exact.

The experimental comparisons do not adequately isolate algorithmic improvements. Only the proposed breakpoint procedure uses compiled C++, and the polishing experiments give OBCD an additional ten seconds without a matched baseline-continuation control. Repeated-run variability and baseline tuning details are absent. Experiments exclusively use k=2 and n≤1000, with no direct ablations establishing the benefits of reflections or the fifth-order solver.

Reproducibility contains a concrete inconsistency: the nonnegative initialization sets each active column entry to 1/|G_i|, giving squared column norm 1/|G_i| rather than 1. Since the update preserves the Gram matrix, this initialization cannot produce the reported orthogonality accuracy without an unreported correction. Code availability is only described through an unspecified research webpage, and preprocessing, sampled indices, and construction of E in the eigenvalue experiments are insufficiently specified.
